articles.title: ‘Alien-cortical’ mice: Can human brain cells grow inside animals?
articles.summary: Modified mice with human brain cells ignite debates over neurohybrids and the future of cross-species medical research.
articles.body:
In a laboratory in California, in the United States, mice are scurrying around their cages, as mice do. But inside their brains are millions of working human neurons.

Researchers at Stanford University have implanted lab-grown human cells into mice genetically engineered to lack parts of their brains, including the cerebral cortex, the outer region that plays a major role in perception, movement, decision-making and attention.

According to a study published in Nature, these so-called “alien-cortical mice” may offer a new way to study neural circuits and brain disorders such as schizophrenia, cerebral palsy and dementia.

Putting human brain tissue inside an animal sounds like something out of Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, but how “human” are these mice, really? And what have the researchers found?

Researchers genetically modified the mice so they were born and grew without most of the cerebral cortex and the neighbouring hippocampus, which are needed for movement, learning and memory.

When the animals were two days old, researchers injected human “organoids” into the empty spaces. Organoids are miniature masses of cells grown in a laboratory from stem cells or tumour tissue which mimic real human organs. Each was grown from healthy donors’ stem cells and holds about 100,000 human cells.

Overall, researchers removed about 14 million mouse neurons and added about 4 million human ones.

This is not the same thing as a brain transplant, and the animals are not “mice that think like humans”, the researchers emphasised.

They tried the transplants on 29 mice, and it worked on 25 of them.

Within three months, the human tissue had grown about five times larger inside the mice’s brains, connected to their blood supply and filled more than 90 percent of the cavities.

The “alien cortex” mice walked and vocalised mostly normally, even though human tissue made up about half their brain volume.

In a maze test, mice without the implanted human tissue kept getting lost, however, while those with human cells did better, suggesting the human tissue contributed to cognition.

Unexpectedly, some of the tissue developed into von Economo neurons, which are long, rare cells normally absent in mice and almost impossible to make in a lab. They are found in highly social animals such as humans, apes, whales and elephants.

The experiment might also help explain cerebral palsy.

While human infants can suffer from oxygen deprivation as a result of more frequent complications during much longer and trickier childbirth, mice infants rarely do, which has made the condition hard to study in rodents.

When the modified mice in this case were exposed to low oxygen, they showed brain damage, an altered gait and poor limb coordination.

Human brain diseases are among the hardest conditions to study. The brain contains about 86 billion nerve cells linked by trillions of connections. Ethical and safety barriers, along with the brain’s high biological complexity, limit access to living human brain tissue.

Scientists have spent years growing “organoids” instead: Small clusters of human nerve cells grown in a lab. But they are not brains in a dish. They lack the connections, inputs and environment of a living brain.

Sergiu Pasca, senior author of the research paper and a professor of psychiatry and behavioural sciences at Stanford University, said this has the potential to give researchers unprecedented insight into the human brain.

“For the past two decades, there’s been a quest to try to build models of the human brain outside of the human body,” he said.

“This is not going to replace all the models we had before, but it’s going to provide us access to other aspects of human brain function that would be very difficult to study otherwise.”

As research into brain organoids advances, so too do calls for clear regulations and oversight, given the sensitive ethical questions raised by these technologies.

These questions centre on the possibility that cell clusters and brains grown outside the bodies of their owners possess the capacity for sensation or consciousness, and whether this can be scientifically verified.

The researchers stopped the experiments when the human nerve cells implanted in the brains of mice were six months old, before they could form more neural connections with the animals’ brains, and before any signs of consciousness appeared.

John Evans, a sociology professor at the University of California, San Diego, who was not involved in the study, said this experiment does not in itself raise major ethical issues, but it provides evidence that other animals could be created that might raise more serious ethical concerns.

Setting clear boundaries for this research remains a challenge.

According to Evans, the problem lies in the lack of clear stopping points on the gradual path that research could take from mice to non-human primates.

Accordingly, he suggested that researchers should not go beyond rodents for the time being, in order to avoid creating neurohybrid organisms that combine human and animal characteristics and could provoke an ethical controversy.

articles.title: Birds, love letters and silver - what sweeps find in chimneys
articles.summary: Jaw-dropping objects, dirty secrets and trapped wildlife are among the items found up chimneys.
articles.body:
A bundle of love letters tied with a red ribbon, a child's party balloon and a nine-foot scaffold pole are just some of the strange items discovered inside British chimneys, according to sweeps.

Throw in four tonnes of nesting material and a pile of pornographic magazines and it seems there is never a dull day being a chimney sweep.

"You name it, we found it," said Martin Glynn, president of the National Association of Chimney Sweeps.

The recent discovery by a Cornwall sweep of a live owl that got stuck in a chimney stove came during a routine clean at a home in Polperro, Cornwall.

So the BBC asked chimney sweeps what other objects and animals they had found stuck or stashed away.

Among Glynn's most unusual discoveries was a bundle of love letters exchanged between a homeowner and a man in Belgium which had been hidden in a chimney.

The sweep also found builders' boots, hammers and a scaffold pole that had fallen down a chimney while roofing work was being carried out.

In Devon, chimney sweep Jonathan Miles said one of the strangest things he had found was a "mummified bag of chips" alongside a stack of pornographic magazines inside a chimney in Topsham.

Miles, who runs Best Chimney Clean in Exeter, said chimney sweeps often uncovered items that had been deliberately hidden away.

Over the years he has found notes, cigarette packets, coins and letters to Father Christmas. He said he also knew of a London chimney sweep whose father had discovered a gun inside a chimney.

Wildlife is another common cause of call-outs. Miles said he was contacted several times a month to rescue animals that had become trapped inside chimneys, including wood pigeons, squirrels, magpies, starlings and even a seagull.

One recent job at a listed manor house in mid Devon, uncovered what he believed were decades' worth of jackdaw nests.

Alongside huge amounts of nesting material were silver-coloured spoons, sugar tongs, bottle tops and fragments of clay pigeon targets which the birds had collected.

"What was really unusual about this one... we found half a dozen spoons, like, silver-type spoons, sugar tongs, bottle tops and caps," he said.

Miles estimated around four tonnes of nesting material was removed from the property, a task that took two chimney sweeps about 16 hours to complete.

If birds are nesting in a chimney, they should be left alone because wild birds, their eggs and their young are protected by law. It is also worth remembering that some species raise more than one brood each year, so a nest may still be active even if birds have not been seen using it recently.

If a homeowner wants to stop birds returning the following year, they should wait until the nest has been completely abandoned and then use a professional to fit a wire mesh guard or chimney cowl. This helps prevent future nesting without disturbing protected birds.

A fully feathered adult bird that has become trapped in a chimney can usually be removed and released during daylight hours if it is alert, active, uninjured and shows no signs of being affected by soot.

However, birds should not be removed if they appear dazed, injured, have been trapped for several hours, have soot in their eyes, or seem to be young nestlings or fledglings. In these cases, the quickest way to get help is to contact a vet.

Open all windows and any external doors in the room.

Pull back curtains to maximise natural light.

Leave the room and monitor the situation for up to two hours.

If the bird is flying around indoors, leave only one obvious exit route open where possible.

Switch off indoor lights and close curtains over any windows you do not want the bird to fly towards.

Place a torch at the bottom of the chimney to help the bird see the room below, but do not shine it directly at the bird.

Birds that enter a room from a chimney will usually head towards the brightest light source. Creating a single clear escape route can help them find their way outside without becoming confused.

If the bird escapes but appears sick or injured, seek veterinary help. Never try to catch a flying injured bird by throwing a towel or blanket over it, as this could make existing injuries worse.

While unusual discoveries can make for memorable stories, both sweeps stressed that chimney maintenance is primarily about safety.

Glynn warned blocked chimneys could have serious consequences. He described one incident in London where a birthday balloon became lodged in a chimney after a gas fire was lit.

"It nearly gassed and poisoned the family because the balloon literally blocked the chimney," he said.

Miles said qualified chimney sweeps took their safety role seriously and worked to prevent chimney fires and carbon monoxide risks.

"Our primary role is about safety. It's about making sure that if anyone's running an open fire or a wood burner or multi-fuel stove, or any sort of solid heating device... it is safe to use," he said.

Glynn added: "A clean chimney is a safer chimney."

articles.title: Work to restore New Forest wildfire site gets under way
articles.summary: Work begins to restore nature to part of the New Forest destroyed by a summer wildfire.
articles.body:
Restoration work has begun at the site of a devastating wildfire in a national park.

More than 1 sq km (247 acres) of the New Forest was destroyed after a fire spread from a blazing van on 9 August.

The fire caused damage to rare heathland and an ancient woodland, as well as burning through a surface layer of peat in some of the boggy areas, reducing their ability to store carbon.

Forestry England said it had begun a long-term project to help nature return to the affected area, with specialist teams starting work to protect the most vulnerable areas ahead of winter and helping to reseed areas of heather.

The agency, which is responsible for managing publicly owned forests in England, said the blaze spread across the heathland, removing all the plants on the surface before travelling underground to destroy layers of roots and seed banks.

At its height, the fire closed the A31 - a major tourist and commuter route between Hampshire and Dorset - for nearly two weeks.

It came during an exceptionally busy summer for Hampshire and Isle of Wight firefighters, and is estimated to have cost the fire service £600,000 .

Forestry England's Dave Morris said: "The scene immediately after the fire had gone through this part of the forest is something I will never forget."

Morris added: "Large areas were reduced to piles of charcoal, burnt soils and torched trees. At that time, it was difficult to imagine it would ever fully return to a place where nature could thrive.

"Undeterred, our specialist staff immediately got to work to see how we could help the area recover."

Heather full of seed was harvested from nearby parts of the forest and has been spread across the worst-affected parts of the fire site to form a "protective mat" and encourage new plants to grow.

Forestry England used the same technique after part of the New Forest was destroyed by a previous wildfire in 1989.

"Almost 40 years later, this area is now thriving and has been fully restored," it said.

Teams are also looking at ways to protect the vulnerable roots of ancient beech and oak trees damaged in this summer's fire.

The boggy areas of the fire site sustained the least damage, acting as a barrier to help slow the blaze from moving more widely across forest, and have recovered the quickest.

"The fire has reminded us that nature is remarkably resilient and in the boggy parts of the fire area we can already see plants and wildlife returning," said Morris.

"It will take many decades for the area burnt by the fire to recover completely but, with the right help at the right time, we can give it the helping hand it needs."

articles.title: Drought and hot weather threatens future of Christmas trees, farmer warns
articles.summary: Oxfordshire farmer warns summer drought could affect Christmas tree production for years to come
articles.body:
"If we have more summers like the last two, we'll be struggling as a nation to produce enough Christmas trees."

Andrew Ingram owns The Tree Barn in Christmas Common, Oxfordshire, which is home to about 120,000 trees.

But this year's hot summer and drought has reduced that total by more than a thousand.

"It's been an extraordinary year," he said. "We planted in perfect conditions in March and then it didn't rain for 12 weeks until the first week of June.

"Then after that it didn't rain until September, it's very depressing."

Russell Parkins, chair of the British Christmas Tree Association, agreed that growers across the country had faced a "tough year".

He said his organisation was working on "ongoing research to help ensure British-grown Christmas trees continue to thrive in a changing climate".

The full impact of the drought is unlikely to be felt immediately, with the biggest consequences potentially coming in years to come.

Some Christmas trees can take up to nine years to reach six feet tall, meaning the loss of young saplings could affect production well into the next decade.

"A transplant we put in will be around a year old and it's replacing a tree that is three to four years old so that's affecting production and could lead to shortages in the future," said Ingram.

"It means we have to walk the rows, pull out the dead trees, replace them by hand…it's a laborious job, a time consuming job and an expensive job."

"We tend to plant in the spring but that's becoming a more dangerous time to plant," Ingram said.

"It would be better to plant in Autumn because that allows the tree to get established and routed in through the winter."

He said there were also concerns that warmer temperatures this winter could mean less frosts.

Frosts help to keep Christmas trees in a dormant state, helping them to hold onto their needles for longer once they've entered our homes for the festive period.

"I think there's a real danger we'll see more trees losing their needles this year," Ingram said.

"We're going to have to figure out ways to carry on growing even if the weather turns against us."

articles.title: An NHS manager allegedly claimed her mother had died to obtain compassionate leave, then took another job 170 miles away, paying £550 a day
articles.summary: An NHS HR manager told her employer that her mother had died, took compassionate leave, and began a new job in Birmingham paying £550 a day, a court has
articles.body: An NHS HR manager told her employer that her mother had died, took compassionate leave, and began a new job in Birmingham paying £550 a day, a court has heard. Leanne Underhill, 46, worked at University Hospitals Dorset. The trust became suspicious in May 2024 when a recruitment firm asked for a reference. She admitted the lie in November 2024. On 16 February 2026, Poole Magistrates’ Court sentenced her for three counts of fraud by false representation. The court heard she had dishonestly obtained £2,258 in wages, and she was ordered to repay £6,948.25 in £150 monthly instalments.Why did an NHS manager allegedly fake her mother's deathAccording to Independent, Underhill had in fact secured another HR role at Birmingham City Council, 170 miles from the trust. Mr Salame told the court she started there on a daily rate of £550. The NHSCFA states that during the same period she presented fit notes despite being fit to work, and that she undertook additional employment for part of that time.The trust became suspicious at the end of May, according to The Independent, when the recruitment firm Morgan Law asked it for a reference for the Birmingham job. Mr Salame said her contract at the council was then terminated. The NHS Counter Fraud team began an investigation and interviewed her in July 2024.How did the NHS manager admit to faking her mother's deathAccording to NHSCFA, Underhill, then 46, admitted in the July interview that she had started a job elsewhere. She said she could not return to the trust because of problems with her line manager. She ended the voluntary interview when asked about her mother and the bereavement leave.At a second interview in November 2024, she admitted that her mother had not died, according to The Independent. The paper reports that she blamed acute mental health problems stemming from drink and drug issues. The NHSCFA says she pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation at Poole Magistrates' Court on 4 December 2025.How was the NHS manager ordered to repay £6,948Underhill was sentenced at Poole Magistrates' Court on Monday 16 February 2026, the NHSCFA says. The Independent reports she was sentenced for three counts of fraud by false representation covering May and June 2024. The court heard that she had dishonestly obtained £2,258 in wages, and that the investigation had cost the NHS £4,940. She had already repaid £250, and Deputy Judge Roderick Hine ordered her to pay the remaining £6,948 as compensation. The NHSCFA gives the figure as £6,948.25, covering her full salary overpayment and the full investigation costs. She is to repay it in monthly instalments of £150, starting on 1 March 2026.The Independent reports that Underhill, who represented herself, told the court she was "deeply ashamed" of her actions. The NHSCFA quotes Pete Papworth, the trust's chief finance officer, as saying that "The NHS is under huge financial pressure". articles.title: ‘Experimenting on 1.3 billion people’: Priyank Kharge alleges excess ethanol blending in E20 petrol
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Karnataka minister Priyank Kharge on Saturday accused the Central government of misleading people over ethanol blending in petrol, alleging
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Karnataka minister Priyank Kharge on Saturday accused the Central government of misleading people over ethanol blending in petrol, alleging that reports from government-accredited laboratories showed ethanol content exceeding the limits announced by the Centre.Kharge also alleged that the ethanol-blending programme was being used to benefit companies linked to the families of Union ministers. He claimed that some laboratory reports had indicated blending levels of up to 35-40 per cent, while others showed 31 per cent."The Government of India is lying through its teeth to the people. Very clearly, they had said that it (ethanol) will not be blended beyond a certain capacity, but NABL reports have proved that the ethanol blending is crossing the permissible limits, or at least the set limits that the govt had proclaimed. It's up to 35%, 40% in some cases. The lab reports are endorsed by laboratories that are accredited by the Govt of India," he said, as quoted by news agency ANI.The minister alleged that the policy was intended to facilitate certain companies. "This entire ethanol blending has been done only to facilitate companies of Union ministers," he said.Rahul Gandhi questions E20 petrol content; oil companies dispute Karnataka findingsKharge's remarks came after Congress leader Rahul Gandhi accused the Centre of failing to disclose the actual ethanol content in petrol being sold across the country.In a post on X, the Congress MP said tests conducted on petrol samples collected from seven districts in Karnataka had found ethanol levels above the prescribed 20 per cent.He claimed that 11 of the 14 samples tested contained more than 20 per cent ethanol, with samples from Indian Oil Corporation (IOCL) and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL) recording 31.2 per cent and 30.5 per cent, respectively.Karnataka food, civil supplies, consumer affairs and legal metrology minister Rizwan Arshad had said the samples were collected from Bengaluru, Kolar, Chikkaballapura, Bengaluru Rural, Ramanagara, Mangaluru and Tumakuru. The tests were conducted by the NABL-accredited and ISO-certified Shriram Research Institute in Bengaluru.However, state-run oil marketing companies IOC, BPCL and HPCL have disputed the Karnataka government's findings. In a joint statement, the companies said E20 petrol supplied across their retail networks, including in Karnataka, complied with the Bureau of Indian Standards' IS 17021 specifications, which prescribe an ethanol content of 19-21 per cent.The companies also questioned the sampling and testing procedures used by the state government, saying the third-party laboratory certificates did not provide sufficient details of the testing methodology to independently verify the reported levels.Kharge questions Centre's stand on ethanol blendingKharge referred to the Solicitor General's submission before the Supreme Court, in which ethanol blending was described as an experiment that was not being implemented across the country."If you recollect, the Solicitor General had told in the Supreme Court that this entire ethanol blending was an experiment and is not happening throughout the country, but if you actually look closely, you are experimenting on 1.3 billion people. How does that even work? So it is very clear that this Government of India has been lying to its own people only for profiteering," he said.He also cited the 31 per cent blending figure and referred to concerns raised by vehicle manufacturers over possible damage to vehicles."This is cheating the public, cheating being done for the company of a central minister's son. What is the NABL organisation saying? 31% blending is happening. They themselves are saying. Vehicle organisations have written letters saying vehicles are getting damaged; they have also threatened and intimidated, and got it withdrawn. Yesterday Rizwan Arshad spoke about NABL, where are BJP people now?" Kharge said.Rahul has also claimed that excessive ethanol blending could affect vehicle performance, leading to lower mileage and higher maintenance costs. He questioned the absence of labels at fuel stations disclosing the ethanol content of petrol.India's ethanol-blending programme began with a pilot initiative in 2001 and aims to reduce dependence on imported crude oil, strengthen domestic agricultural value chains and improve energy security.According to petroleum ministry data cited by the oil marketing companies, the programme has generated foreign exchange savings of more than Rs 1.97 lakh crore since the 2014-15 ethanol supply year, substituted around 316 lakh metric tonnes of crude oil and reduced carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 952 lakh metric tonnes.During the 2025-26 ethanol supply year, which ended on October 31, 2026, the three public sector oil marketing companies procured 1,089 crore litres of ethanol and blended 1,134 crore litres against petrol sales of around 5,673 crore litres.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: DIVINE’s Fifty Nine Records steps into the spotlight with a 17-artist roster

articles.body: India, November 4, 2026: Fifty Nine Records, the multi-genre, multi-lingual music imprint launched by rapper DIVINE, is making its official debut after operating behind the scenes since 2024. The label aims to bring emerging musical voices from across India to the forefront, cutting across regional, linguistic and genre boundaries.The announcement comes on the back of a major digital breakthrough for its latest release, ‘Filam’ by Haryanvi rapper Duryodhan Rana. Originally released in August 2025, the track has witnessed a sudden surge in popularity, with over 50% of its total Spotify streams coming in the last four weeks. It climbed to No. 122 on Spotify India's Daily Top 200 chart on October 30, while featuring in over 5 lakh Instagram Reels.Built to provide independent artists with a platform beyond geographical and musical limitations, the imprint has spent the past two years developing a roster of 17 artists. Its catalogue comprises 35 tracks across hip-hop, drill, R&B, regional pop and folk-pop, with music spanning languages such as Hindi, Haryanvi and Bhojpuri. Despite its low-key launch, the venture has already clocked over 125 million audio streams, 55 million YouTube views and more than 30 billion views across short-video platforms.‘Filam’ is not the label's first digital success. Bhartiya Radio's ‘Mafia’ generated over 25 lakh Instagram Reels, while Duryodhan Rana's earlier release ‘Bhid Mat’ crossed 12 million Spotify streams. Knojia's critically acclaimed track ‘Nazra’ has also contributed to the imprint's growing regional footprint.Explaining the vision behind the venture, Chaitanya Kataria, CEO, Gully Gang Entertainment, said, “The idea for Fifty Nine Records was born out of our intention to platform emerging artists across India without limitations to genre and language. As our country's digital footprint expands, so does the discovery of creativity across it. This imprint allows us to do that. The inspiration behind the name comes from the pincode (400059) of Andheri East's JB Nagar, where DIVINE grew up and honed his skills as an emerging artist before becoming the superstar he is today.”Amit Ojha, Head – Label Imprints, added, “We intentionally kept Fifty Nine under wraps so the music could speak for itself first. Our roster is now charting nationally and building hyper-engaged audiences far beyond their home regions, all while staying entirely true to their localised sounds. Duryodhan's chart entry is the blueprint, and he is only the beginning of what we have in the pipeline.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Will Trump strike nuclear sites again as Iran engages ‘cognitive warfare’?
articles.summary: The US president has been sending mixed messages after his party suffered a defeat at the midterm elections.
articles.body:
Since Tuesday’s midterms, United States President Donald Trump has shifted his rhetoric between threatening Iran and suggesting that a resolution to the war is near.

After accepting a devastating Republican defeat at the elections and acknowledging his deeply unpopular war on Iran was partly to blame, Trump told reporters on Thursday the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts.

On Friday, US forces carried out what he described as “minor strikes” against Iranian air defence systems, and Iran’s official news agency, IRNA, reported two missiles had again struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

But on the same day, Trump said the US administration is talking to Iranian representatives and told reporters, “We’ve made a lot of progress with Iran.”

Observers say Iran’s intransigence over the demands it has made of the US before it will reopen the critical Strait of Hormuz to shipping, balanced against Trump’s drubbing at the US midterms, has painted the US president into a tricky corner over what to do next.

So besides the mixed messages from him, what is happening on the ground and what is most likely to happen next? Here is what we know:

Trump said it is, several times, on Friday.

“We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal,” the US president told reporters, without providing further details.

On Saturday, Majed al-Ansari, spokesperson for the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs, dismissed claims circulating on X that negotiations between the US and Iran had failed, warning that such claims benefit “only those seeking to prolong the war”.

Why has the US struck Qeshm Island again?

Trump confirmed the US had carried out military strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Friday, while Iranian state media reported two missile strikes in the Suza area of the island. This follows what the US described as “ defensive strikes ” on the island, considered to be a primary naval base for Iran and housing “ missile cities “, earlier this week.

The US says it is targeting missile launch systems. On Monday, an unnamed US official told AP that Washington had conducted the strikes to prevent “Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets”.

Iranian state broadcaster IRIB also reported an Iranian army statement, saying the country’s air defence forces intercepted and destroyed a US MQ-9 drone over the island.

In response to reports of explosions heard on Qeshm, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, said the situation is “relatively calm”.

Iran is distributing iodine tablets to communities near its nuclear facilities, the United Kingdom’s Times newspaper reported, quoting a Ministry of Health official who said, “Trump can no longer be trusted. He may go through with this crime.”

The official added that during every war, Iran has tried to distribute the tablets within a radius of 2-3km (1.2-1.9 miles) of nuclear facilities.

Iodine tablets are used to protect the thyroid gland from radiation.

The newspaper reported that an Iranian political journalist said officials had been told at a recent briefing that a US nuclear strike on the heavily fortified Pickaxe Mountain site, beneath which is believed to be a large complex of tunnels and facilities, is being seriously considered.

The Young Journalists Club (YJC) news agency in Iran also reported on Friday that health authorities have been distributing iodine tablets to residents of the southern city of Bushehr, home to the country’s only operational nuclear power plant.

The US State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme meanwhile announced on Friday it is offering a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear programme, including its facilities, equipment and associated personnel.

Why does Trump have such a dilemma about what to do next?

Trump is facing strong opposition to the war at home from voters and from within his own Republican Party, angered by the loss of control of both houses of Congress at the elections. But he has long insisted he will not accept Iran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restarting peace talks. These include lifting sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets, ending the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, and guaranteeing an end to attacks.

Facing a decision on whether to bend to these now or risk further wrath at home by pushing ahead with attacks, Trump is in a tight spot.

Iran’s strategy in responding to US-Israeli attacks by attacking bases and facilities in neighbouring Gulf countries has weakened Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at home and narrowed their options in any confrontation with Iran, Hassan Ahmadian, an associate professor at the University of Tehran and deputy director of the Middle East Scientific and Strategic Studies Center, wrote on X.

Now, Iran is threatening to widen its responsive strikes, suggesting countries beyond the Gulf could be hit next.

Ahmadian said Trump has no clear idea of how a limited strike would end, “and that’s what feeds his personal hesitation and the splintered views of his circle on Iran”.

“None of this means he won’t attack Iran,” he said, but Trump wants to be sure a strike is worth it, gives him “a respectable way out”, and does not lead Iran to widen its response into an all-out war against US forces and Israel.

Iran’s “cognitive warfare” has kept Trump “in the fog” about what would follow a limited war, Ahmadian said, and he “needs to make up his mind fast, before next January”.

No one seems certain, but the US and Iran say they are prepared for any eventuality.

The US news website Axios quoted a US official saying that CENTCOM is preparing for the resumption of major military operations in Iran, and that it is just waiting on orders from Washington.

Tehran warned it will retaliate on a wider scale than it has done so far if the US resumes the war.

“In the event of a new aggression, any country or force that helps America attack Iran can be a legitimate target of the Islamic Republic,” a spokesman for the supreme adviser to the commander of the Aerospace Force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Thursday.

Iran has also previously warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) facilities across the Gulf region could be attacked if war erupts again.

But behind the bombastic rhetoric, diplomatic efforts continue.

On Thursday, Iran offered the US a new nuclear and peace proposal via Qatari mediators, to be discussed only after Washington meets Tehran’s seven demands, a senior Iranian official told the Reuters news agency. The US is examining the proposal, Reuters reported.

Former Iranian diplomat Hadi Afghahi told Al Jazeera that Tehran can ease the path to a settlement if the US also shows flexibility. He argued that Trump “really does not want to go to war, because war again will cost him more”.

However, Afghahi cautioned that Trump “is still surrounded by a group of hawks”, including the energy and treasury secretaries.

Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, during a public interview at Oxford University on Friday, urged the US and Iran not to wait for a “perfect moment” to reach a deal to end the war.
